For eligible tables, Oracle 11g can optimize adding a column with a constant default and a NOT NULL constraint. Oracle stores the default in metadata rather than physically populating every existing row. Restrictions apply; this is not a guarantee for every defaulted-column operation.


CREATE TABLE f03_defaults AS
SELECT LEVEL AS id, RPAD('x', 100, 'x') AS payload
FROM dual
CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 100000;

SELECT bytes AS bytes_before
FROM user_segments
WHERE segment_name = 'F03_DEFAULTS'
  AND segment_type = 'TABLE';

ALTER TABLE f03_defaults ADD (
    status VARCHAR2(10) DEFAULT 'NEW' NOT NULL
);

SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM f03_defaults
GROUP BY status;

SELECT column_name, nullable, data_default
FROM user_tab_columns
WHERE table_name = 'F03_DEFAULTS'
  AND column_name = 'STATUS';

SELECT bytes AS bytes_after
FROM user_segments
WHERE segment_name = 'F03_DEFAULTS'
  AND segment_type = 'TABLE';



All 100,000 rows return NEW, and NULLABLE is N. On an eligible configuration, the change should be fast and allocated segment bytes will typically remain unchanged.



Visible default values confirm SQL semantics. Timing and unchanged allocated bytes are supporting observations, not conclusive proof that no rows were physically modified.

text:
The right-hand query of an APPLY join can reference a table to its left. This makes patterns such as selecting the highest-paid employee in each department easier to express.
CROSS APPLY drops left-hand rows with no right-hand result. OUTER APPLY preserves them and supplies nulls for right-hand columns.


CREATE TABLE c12_departments (
    department_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
    department_name VARCHAR2(50) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE c12_employees (
    employee_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
    department_id NUMBER NOT NULL,
    employee_name VARCHAR2(50) NOT NULL,
    salary NUMBER(10,2) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT c12_emp_dept_fk FOREIGN KEY (department_id)
        REFERENCES c12_departments (department_id)
);

INSERT INTO c12_departments VALUES (10, 'Engineering');
INSERT INTO c12_departments VALUES (20, 'Sales');
INSERT INTO c12_departments VALUES (30, 'Support');

INSERT INTO c12_employees VALUES (1, 10, 'Amina', 9000);
INSERT INTO c12_employees VALUES (2, 10, 'Omar', 8000);
INSERT INTO c12_employees VALUES (3, 20, 'Sara', 7000);
COMMIT;

-- Departments with a matching employee only.
SELECT d.department_name, e.employee_name, e.salary
FROM c12_departments d
CROSS APPLY (
    SELECT x.employee_name, x.salary
    FROM c12_employees x
    WHERE x.department_id = d.department_id
    ORDER BY x.salary DESC, x.employee_id
    FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY
) e
ORDER BY d.department_id;

-- Preserve departments with no employees as well.
SELECT d.department_name, e.employee_name, e.salary
FROM c12_departments d
OUTER APPLY (
    SELECT x.employee_name, x.salary
    FROM c12_employees x
    WHERE x.department_id = d.department_id
    ORDER BY x.salary DESC, x.employee_id
    FETCH FIRST 1 ROW ONLY
) e
ORDER BY d.department_id;



The CROSS APPLY query returns:
DEPARTMENT_NAME  EMPLOYEE_NAME  SALARY
--------------- -------------  ------
Engineering      Amina          9000
Sales            Sara           7000
The OUTER APPLY query also returns:
Support          (null)         (null)



The correlated subquery describes the desired result for each department. The optimizer determines the physical execution strategy; the syntax does not promise a particular procedural execution order or superior performance.

Completed Operational Automations
The following nine automations have been completed and are running successfully.
Their successful operation refers to the automation workflows themselves. Monitoring reports may still identify failed backups, unavailable applications, or other conditions requiring investigation.

Automated the collection and presentation of key database, application, and server-health information.
The reporting scope includes:

Instance status and database information.
Database size and space utilization.
ASM disk-group utilization.
Tablespace capacity and low-free-space checks, including checks for less than 5% available space.
Archive log statistics.
Daily RMAN backup status.
Top SQL queries by resource consumption.
Sessions with high physical I/O activity.
EBS Concurrent Manager status.
Database export-backup verification.
Disk-space details for database and application servers.

This provides a consolidated starting point for daily operational review and helps identify storage constraints, backup issues, and resource-intensive activity.
The reporting approach is modular, allowing additional checks, databases, and servers to be incorporated as requirements evolve.


2. Daily Auditing Reports
Automated daily auditing reports to improve visibility and traceability of database activities.
The reports support audit review and compliance-related activities without requiring the same information to be gathered manually.
The approach accommodates different database audit configurations and user-activity reporting requirements.


3. Automated Database Table Statistics Gathering
Automated statistics gathering for selected database tables to keep optimizer statistics current.
This standardizes a recurring maintenance activity and supports consistent query-optimization inputs.
Additional tables can be included as application and maintenance requirements change.


4. Daily Alert Log Monitoring
Automated database alert-log review to surface errors and warnings requiring attention.
The workflow produces log outputs that support investigation without requiring administrators to manually inspect every full alert log.
The monitoring approach can accommodate different log locations, formats, and alert levels across environments.


5. Application Availability Reporting
Automated application endpoint checks and generated reports showing availability status and response information.
The reporting includes:

A consolidated application-health view.
Working, warning, and failed status categories.
Response information for individual checks.
A separate exception report highlighting failed or warning entries.

This helps direct operational attention to services requiring investigation.
Availability results reflect the checks performed at the reporting time; they are not a guarantee of continuous application availability.
The configuration-based approach allows additional application endpoints and environments to be included.


6. Daily Table Growth Tracking
Automated daily table-growth tracking to improve visibility into changing storage consumption.
The reports support:

Reviewing growth trends.
Identifying unusual increases.
Planning future capacity.
Prioritizing storage investigations.

The approach can be reused across databases, environments, and projects.


7. Tableau Log Management
Automated Tableau log housekeeping on Windows servers to reclaim space and support reliable platform operations.
This reduces recurring manual cleanup and helps prevent unnecessary log accumulation from consuming available disk capacity.
The housekeeping approach can be adapted to other tools with similar log-management requirements.


8. Table and Tablespace Space Management
Automated space-management activities to support table growth and reduce dependence on repeated manual intervention.
The objective is to address capacity constraints before they interrupt database operations.
This complements growth tracking and low-space reporting by bringing recurring space-management work into an automated workflow.


9. Database Alert Log Management
Automated scheduled database alert-log housekeeping, including monthly purging and backup for future reference.
This is separate from daily alert-log monitoring:

Monitoring identifies errors and warnings.
Housekeeping manages accumulated log files and retained copies.

The approach can be applied across multiple database environments.

title: VEncoder: A macOS Application for Efficient Video Encoding
text:
I developed VEncoder, a macOS application designed to make video compression and batch conversion easier to manage.
The goal was to reduce video file sizes while retaining the original resolution, bring common encoding settings into one interface, and simplify the processing of multiple videos.
VEncoder combines an FFmpeg-based conversion workflow with codec selection, configurable parallel processing, language preferences, output-folder management, and a searchable conversion queue.

title: VEncoder: A macOS Application for Efficient Video Encoding
text:
The Challenge
Managing a growing video collection can involve more than choosing a smaller output format. Different files may require different encoding settings, contain multiple language tracks, or need to be processed in a particular order.
Repeatedly configuring individual conversions also makes larger batches time-consuming to organize.
I wanted to bring these tasks into a single macOS application that could:

Reduce storage requirements without requiring a lower resolution.
Provide a choice of target video codecs.
Process multiple videos through a managed queue.
Allow control over the number of simultaneous conversions.
Simplify language selection and output-folder configuration.
Make progress and processing status visible in one place.

title: VEncoder: A macOS Application for Efficient Video Encoding
section: The Solution: A Centralized Video Conversion Workflow
text:
The Solution: A Centralized Video Conversion Workflow
VEncoder provides a graphical interface for configuring and managing video conversions, rather than requiring users to prepare a separate command for each file.
The interface brings together encoding settings, input videos, output locations, and queue controls.



VEncoder welcome screen introducing the application and its main capabilities.


The workflow is organized around five steps:

Add videos or folders.
Select a target codec.
Configure resolution, language preferences, and parallel processing.
Choose output folders.
Start conversion and monitor the queue.

title: VEncoder: A macOS Application for Efficient Video Encoding
text:
Encoding Controls

Multiple Target Codecs
The interface provides the following target-codec options:

H.264 / AVC.
H.265 / HEVC.
VP9.
AV1.
H.266 / VVC.

These options allow the encoding workflow to accommodate different storage and playback requirements.
The interface also includes codec information popovers, giving users additional context when choosing an encoding format.



VEncoder codec-selection panel with an information popover for H.265 / HEVC.


The available encoder and hardware-acceleration path depend on the installed FFmpeg build, selected codec, and capabilities of the Mac. A codec appearing in the interface does not mean every Mac can encode it using hardware acceleration.


Retaining Source Resolution
VEncoder includes a “Same as source” resolution option, allowing users to retain the input video’s frame dimensions during conversion.
This supports the project’s main objective: reducing file size without requiring a reduction in resolution.
Preserving resolution does not mean the output is lossless. The final file size and visual quality still depend on the source material and encoding settings.


Language and Subtitle Preferences
A native-language preference helps guide automatic language and subtitle selection.
The interface accepts a short language code, bringing this preference into the conversion setup rather than requiring users to configure it separately for each video.


Configurable Parallel Processing
The parallel-process control allows users to choose how many conversions run simultaneously.
This provides a way to tune batch processing to the available system resources. Hardware acceleration, where supported, can complement this workflow, but parallel processing and hardware acceleration are separate capabilities.

text:

The result: approximately 41% less execution time, reducing weekly database cloning from 11 hours to 6.5 hours and saving 4.5 hours each week.

title: Automating Oracle Database Recovery and Cloning
text:
The Challenge
Database recovery and cloning involved multiple manual steps, operational dependencies, and repeated intervention. Administrators had to manage several related operations separately, increasing the effort required to complete the overall workflow.
The main challenges were:

Repeating the same recovery and cloning procedures each week.
Coordinating individual operations and their dependencies.
Maintaining consistent execution across multiple steps.
Reducing opportunities for human error during repetitive tasks.

I wanted a single framework that could support both selective execution and a complete cloning workflow without requiring administrators to repeat the same manual sequence.

title: Automating Oracle Database Recovery and Cloning
section: The Solution: One Framework, Two Execution Modes
text:
The Solution: One Framework, Two Execution Modes
I developed a centralized menu-driven framework with interactive and non-interactive execution modes.
Both modes use standardized execution flows, input handling, and reusable automation logic. The distinction is how much control the administrator needs over the individual steps.

Interactive Mode: Select the Operations You Need
Interactive mode allows the administrator to choose individual operations or select several operations together.
The available operations include:

Database restore and recovery for cloning.
SPFILE migration to ASM.
Archive log configuration for local file systems and ASM.
RAC conversion.
RAC verification.

Administrators can enter comma-separated selections, such as 1,2,3, or use all to select all five operations.



Main menu and interactive execution options, including comma-separated selections.


This mode provides flexibility when only part of the workflow is required, rather than requiring execution of the complete process.


Non-Interactive Mode: Run the Complete Workflow
Non-interactive mode provides a single menu selection to initiate the full workflow, from database restore and recovery through RAC conversion.
Instead of selecting operations individually, the administrator starts the predefined sequence with one selection, reducing the need for repeated manual intervention.



Non-interactive mode with a single option to execute the full workflow.


Here, “non-interactive” refers to the execution workflow after the initial menu selection; the framework still presents a menu to start that workflow.

As historical data accumulated in Hive tables, recurring housekeeping was needed to manage information beyond the required retention period.
Handling these activities manually meant repeatedly reviewing data eligibility and carrying out cleanup operations across the relevant tables.
The objective was to simplify this process while applying a consistent 36-month retention rule.
The main priorities were:

Identify data that had exceeded the required retention period.
Reduce repetitive manual cleanup activities.
Apply the same retention criteria consistently.
Support storage housekeeping as historical data accumulated.
Make recurring purging activities easier to maintain.

title: Automating Hive Data Retention with Python
text:
2. Technical Solution
I developed a Python-based framework to automate the purging workflow for Hive tables containing data older than 36 months.
The framework brought the retention rule and cleanup process into a reusable automation solution rather than treating each cleanup as an independent manual task.

Retention-Based Processing
The central rule was straightforward:

Data older than 36 months becomes eligible for purging under the applicable retention requirements.

The retention period applies to the age of the data, rather than automatically treating a table’s creation date as the age of every record it contains.


Automated Housekeeping
The framework automated recurring purging activities, reducing the need for administrators to repeat the same cleanup steps manually.
This provided a consistent approach to handling expired data across the Hive tables covered by the framework.


Reusable Python Framework
Using a framework-based approach made the automation easier to maintain than a collection of separate, one-time cleanup scripts.
The work focused on turning a recurring administrative requirement into a repeatable operational workflow.

title: NewOracleDB
text:
Oracle Autonomous Database is a managed Oracle database service that automates much of the infrastructure and database administration normally handled by a DBA team. Traditional Oracle databases provide more direct operational control, but their administrators typically take responsibility for installation, configuration, patching, backup execution, and infrastructure maintenance.
Here, “traditional” means a self-managed Oracle database, on premises or on cloud infrastructure. Self-managed Oracle databases can also use substantial automation; the main difference is who operates and remains responsible for it.
Oracle now also uses the name Autonomous AI Database. Capabilities and controls vary by Serverless or Dedicated deployment, infrastructure, compute model, and service version.











Area
Traditional, self-managed Oracle database
Autonomous Database
DBA impact




Administration
The team provisions and maintains the database stack and its automation.
Oracle automates provisioning and much of routine platform administration.
Less installation and infrastructure work; more service configuration and governance.


Performance
DBAs configure resources, investigate SQL, and operate tuning tools.
The service automates many tuning and resource-management tasks; supported workloads can use automatic indexing.
Less routine tuning, but application SQL, data design, and performance validation still matter.


Security
The team operates patching, encryption, access controls, and audit infrastructure.
Oracle manages platform security maintenance and encryption; customers manage access, data exposure, and application security.
Responsibility shifts rather than disappears.


Patching
DBAs plan, test, install, and troubleshoot patches across the stack.
Oracle applies platform and database patches through managed maintenance processes.
Less patch execution; compatibility testing and maintenance awareness remain important.


Backup and recovery
DBAs configure RMAN, storage, retention, monitoring, and restore procedures.
The service performs automatic backups and provides managed restore/recovery workflows.
Focus moves to recovery requirements, retention, restore authorization, and recovery testing.


Scalability
The team provisions capacity and manages infrastructure constraints.
Compute and storage can be adjusted through service controls; supported autoscaling responds to demand within service limits.
Faster capacity changes, with continued cost and quota oversight.






Autonomous Database reduces repetitive work such as database provisioning, backup scheduling, patch installation, and routine platform maintenance. Performance automation helps manage the database without requiring every adjustment to be performed manually.
This does not guarantee that every query is automatically optimal. Poor SQL, unsuitable data models, connection storms, and inefficient application behavior still require investigation. Customers remain responsible for application health and the performance of the queries and updates their applications issue.



Oracle manages security maintenance of the service and automates encryption and patch deployment. This reduces the risk of missing platform patches and removes much of the manual patching workload.
Customers still own important controls:

User accounts, roles, and least-privilege access.
Network access and application connection configuration.
Data classification, audit requirements, and compliance decisions.
Application vulnerabilities and credential handling.

Managed patching is designed to minimize disruption, but do not interpret that as a promise that every maintenance event is invisible to every application. Review deployment-specific maintenance behavior and test client reconnection and retry handling.



Automatic backups remove much of the manual backup-execution work. Managed recovery workflows support recovery to available points within the configured retention period.
For Autonomous Database Serverless, Oracle documents a default automatic-backup retention of 60 days. Eligible ECPU deployments support configuring retention between 1 and 60 days. Verify the applicable service configuration rather than assuming this rule applies to every Autonomous deployment.
A successful managed backup is not a substitute for a recovery plan. DBAs and application owners must still define recovery time and recovery point objectives, verify retention, authorize restores, and rehearse application recovery. Disaster-recovery capabilities and protection choices should be evaluated separately from backup retention.



Autonomous Database makes capacity adjustments easier than procuring and configuring new servers. Supported autoscaling can increase resources as workload demand grows and reduce their use when demand falls.
DBAs still need to monitor resource consumption, service limits, workload concurrency, and cost. Autoscaling is not unlimited capacity, and inefficient workloads can become more expensive rather than automatically become efficient.



The DBA becomes less of an infrastructure operator and more of a service, data, and application-performance administrator.



Installing and maintaining the database platform.
Manually executing platform patches.
Scheduling and operating routine backups.
Performing repetitive infrastructure and capacity operations.





Schema design, SQL review, and application-performance troubleshooting.
Access governance, auditing requirements, and compliance.
Data migration, integration, and application compatibility.
Recovery planning and validation.
Capacity, cost, and service-level management.

Customers also give up some low-level control. Autonomous Database is not an unrestricted host or database installation: supported privileges, parameters, tools, and administrative operations differ from a self-managed system. Validate dependencies on operating-system access and privileged administration before migration.




Autonomous Database reduces operational effort by making Oracle responsible for much of the platform’s operation. Traditional Oracle databases offer more direct control and customization but require the customer to operate and maintain more of the stack.
The choice is a trade-off between managed automation and operational control—not between having a DBA and needing no database expertise.

title: 19c vs. 23ai for DBAs
text:
The biggest DBA-facing differences are architecture, workload management, security controls, recovery operations, and high-availability granularity. Moving from 19c to 23ai can change how you organize databases, grant privileges, diagnose blocking, protect backups, and perform disaster recovery.
This comparison groups the changes into five operational areas and explains their effects on daily administration and migration.


This compares Oracle Database 19c with the 23ai release family, not every feature subsequently added to Oracle AI Database 26ai. Some Oracle documentation URLs now display newer branding or later Release Updates (RUs).
Check each feature against the exact target RU, deployment platform, edition, compatibility setting, and licensing entitlement. A feature available in a later 23ai RU is not necessarily available in the original release.












Area
Oracle Database 19c
Oracle Database 23ai
Practical impact




Architecture
Supports non-CDB and CDB/PDB deployments.
Requires multitenant architecture.
Container-aware administration is mandatory; non-CDBs need conversion.


Performance and workload management
Established relational tuning and automation capabilities.
Adds AI Vector Search, Priority Transactions, and further automation.
New memory/index workloads and application-aware blocking policies.


Security and auditing
Existing privilege and audit configurations are the migration starting point.
Adds SQL Firewall and schema privileges; changes traditional-auditing support.
Revise provisioning, audit policies, and application-change procedures.


Backup and recovery
Existing RMAN and Flashback operational model.
Adds RMAN enhancements, encryption changes under relevant compatibility settings, and separate Flashback log destinations.
Retest runbooks, storage monitoring, key management, and backup tooling.


High availability
Conventional Data Guard protects at database/CDB level.
Adds more granular PDB protection and transaction-recovery fault isolation.
Greater granularity with additional topology and monitoring considerations.








Oracle Database 19c is the last release supporting non-CDB architecture. In 23ai, the supported architecture is a container database containing pluggable databases.
A 19c non-CDB therefore requires both an upgrade and conversion to a PDB. AutoUpgrade can coordinate these operations.

If your 19c database is already a CDB, migration primarily involves upgrading and validating the existing multitenant deployment.
If it is a non-CDB, application connections, administration, monitoring, and recovery procedures must account for its new PDB identity.




The first troubleshooting question becomes: “Which container am I connected to?”
An availability incident may concern one PDB, its service, or its open state rather than the entire CDB. Root-level administration and application-PDB administration must be distinguished.
-- Run with appropriate catalog privileges.
SELECT name, cdb
FROM v$database;

SELECT SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV', 'CON_NAME') AS current_container
FROM dual;

-- Relevant when connected to a CDB.
SELECT con_id, name, open_mode, restricted
FROM v$pdbs
ORDER BY con_id;
These are inventory queries, not an upgrade script. The SQL blocks are displayed as examples and are not executed by Quarto.



Update operating procedures to identify:

The target CDB and PDB for every scheduled job.
Which credentials are common versus local.
Which services applications use.
Which operations affect one PDB versus the shared container.
Which resource and maintenance policies apply to each workload.

Common and local users, roles, and grants are not interchangeable. Scripts that assume a single database context need explicit review.



Do not treat non-CDB conversion as a reversible naming change. Establish and test recovery or fallback before migration. Oracle specifically cautions against relying on read-only tablespaces as a fallback mechanism during the documented non-CDB-to-PDB conversion workflow.
Reference: AutoUpgrade: upgrade and convert a non-CDB to a PDB.






The difference is not simply that every SQL statement runs faster. The more important operational change is a broader workload and control surface:

AI Vector Search introduces vector data, indexes, and similarity-search execution.
Priority Transactions introduces application-aware intervention for row-lock blocking.
Additional automation includes Automatic SecureFiles Shrink and enhancements to In-Memory workload optimization.




DBAs need to understand vector dimensions, index selection, memory requirements, and the trade-off between approximate-search accuracy and execution cost.
Review:

Whether vector workloads share capacity with critical OLTP.
Index-build and maintenance windows.
Memory demand and index availability.
Effects on existing application latency.
Accuracy requirements as well as response time.

Do not assume all vector capabilities exist in the initial 23ai release. Automatic vector-memory management and additional vector-index capabilities arrived in later RUs.



Applications assign transaction priorities and administrators configure wait targets. When a lower-priority transaction blocks higher-priority work beyond the configured threshold, the database can roll back the lower-priority transaction to release its row locks.







Reactive administration
Policy-driven administration




Investigate blocking after an alert.
Define which transactions deserve priority.


Coordinate intervention in a blocking session.
Configure rollback behavior for qualifying lower-priority blockers.


Handle application consequences after intervention.
Test rollback and error handling before enabling policy.



This does not fix long transactions or poor transaction boundaries. It changes failure behavior and requires application-owner approval and testing.



Monitor automation outcomes, not just enabled settings:

Which transactions were rolled back and why.
Whether high-priority response times improved.
Whether maintenance competes with peak workload.
Whether new indexes increase memory and storage pressure.

For licensed and supported In-Memory deployments, automatic feature selection can improve workload optimization. It is not a universal benefit for every database.



Benchmark representative workloads. Compare throughput, latency, blocking, CPU, I/O, and plan stability. Validate existing SQL before introducing optional features so upgrade regressions remain distinguishable from feature-adoption effects.
References:

Oracle release-family new features guide
AI Vector Search documentation
In-Memory enhancements







Oracle 23ai SQL Firewall restricts database activity using authorized SQL and connection contexts. It helps address SQL injection and misuse of stolen credentials, complementing application security and auditing.
The DBA workflow includes:

Capture representative legitimate activity.
Review the resulting allow-list.
Evaluate violations.
Introduce blocking after validation.
Update policies when approved application behavior changes.

Incomplete capture is an operational risk. Routine transactions alone may omit month-end processing, rare reports, or maintenance operations.
Audit violations when blocking is enabled, and include policy administration in security monitoring. Verify licensing and deployment availability before adoption.



Schema privileges provide another authorization scope between individual-object grants and broad database-wide privileges.
This can reduce grant-maintenance work as objects change. However, schema-wide access can still exceed an account’s requirements. Review access by business role rather than mechanically reproducing historical grants.



Unified auditing is not new in 23ai. The important change is the desupport of traditional auditing, with specific treatment of existing settings during upgrades. Existing settings may continue to be honored in an upgraded environment; this is not a reason to retain the old model indefinitely.
Review:

Traditional audit settings and equivalent unified policies.
Audit-trail collection and retention.
SIEM or Audit Vault integration.
Audit volume after changes.
Procedures for policy administration.

23ai also adds unified auditing of individual columns in tables and views, enabling more targeted policies.



Validate both permitted and rejected behavior. A successful login does not prove that privileges, audit records, and firewall policy are correct.
Include scheduled jobs, reporting accounts, support access, deployment tools, and emergency administration in testing.
References:

Oracle SQL Firewall FAQ
Unified audit best-practice guidelines







RMAN remains the foundation for physical backup and recovery. The changes evolve existing workflows rather than replace RMAN with an AI backup engine.



Oracle documents AES-256 in XTS mode for new encrypted backups when COMPATIBLE is set to 23.0.0 or higher, while retaining compatibility with previously configured algorithms.
Distinguish two decisions:

A stronger encryption default does not automatically encrypt all backups.
Changing compatibility and changing encryption configuration are separate operations.

Validate wallet or key access, recovery-host readiness, and restore compatibility rather than relying only on the backup job’s exit status.



23ai introduces a separate destination for Flashback Database logs using:
DB_FLASHBACK_LOG_DEST
DB_FLASHBACK_LOG_DEST_SIZE
Oracle documents disabling and reenabling Flashback logging when changing the destination. Plan the operation around recovery requirements and verify the exact target RU’s procedure.
The benefit is independent placement and capacity management. The consequence is another recovery-critical destination to monitor: an FRA-only dashboard is no longer the complete storage picture.



Oracle’s 23ai RMAN guidance describes:

Oracle-supplied backup modules and aliases.
Configuration support for OCI immutable buckets.
Copying backup sets between SBT destinations.
Simplified transport and platform-migration workflows.
Improved diagnostics and catalog-operation resilience.

Not every convenience is exclusive to 23ai. For example, Oracle notes that the Recovery Appliance backup module is also included starting with 19c RU 19.27. Compare exact RUs, not just major-version names.



Retest with the actual target software and infrastructure:

Restore to an alternate host.
Recover to a required point in time.
Restore encrypted backups using the intended key-management process.
Validate individual-PDB recovery where needed.
Confirm cloud or media-manager integration.

Transport-based migration has workflow-specific limitations. Oracle’s documented PDB transport workflow includes same-endian and local-undo requirements. Do not generalize one supported path into unrestricted cross-platform PDB transport.
References:

RMAN 23ai new features, part 1
RMAN 23ai new features, part 2







Conventional Data Guard protects the CDB as a database. Data Guard per PDB offers more granular protection and role transitions for individual pluggable databases.
This matters when consolidated applications have different availability requirements. A selected PDB can be the unit of protection and role transition rather than treating all PDBs as one application service.
Data Guard per PDB originated in the 21c line and was enhanced in 23ai. It is a difference from 19c, not a feature first invented in 23ai.



Review:

Source and destination CDB infrastructure.
PDB-specific protection and apply state.
Application services and reconnection.
Backup policies after role transitions.
Recovery objectives for each application.

Do not assume feature parity with every conventional Data Guard or Active Data Guard configuration. Validate the exact RU’s restrictions, topology, and licensing requirements.



Automatic Transaction Quarantine isolates problematic transaction recovery so the database can remain available while other work continues. Alerts and diagnostics still require investigation.







Feature
Problem addressed




Priority Transactions
A lower-priority transaction holds row locks that block higher-priority work.


Automatic Transaction Quarantine
A transaction encounters a problematic failure during transaction recovery.



One is a workload policy; the other is a fault-containment mechanism. Neither removes the need to diagnose the underlying cause.



Expand testing beyond startup:

Switchover and failover at the intended protection scope.
Client reconnection and transaction retries.
Backups after role transitions.
Recovery monitoring and alert routing.
Service ownership and operational handoffs.

Measure availability end to end, not merely by whether an instance or PDB is open.
References:

Data Guard new features
Release-family new features guide












Task
What to revise for 23ai




Morning health checks
Identify CDB/PDB scope and inspect applicable recovery, quarantine, and workload-policy alerts.


Access provisioning
Consider schema privileges while preserving least privilege.


Application releases
Review SQL Firewall policies when enabled.


Performance troubleshooting
Separate ordinary SQL regressions from vector pressure and priority-driven rollback.


Capacity planning
Include vector resources and separate Flashback destinations where configured.


Backup monitoring
Review recoverability, encryption keys, and destination accessibility, not just completion.


DR exercises
Test the actual CDB-level or PDB-level protection model and client behavior.


Maintenance automation
Make jobs container-aware and validate features against the installed RU.



Not every item applies to every deployment. Existing monitoring and troubleshooting skills remain essential; new features add context rather than eliminate the need for fundamentals.




Inventory 19c: architecture, RU, options, services, auditing, backups, and HA topology.
Separate required changes from optional adoption. Non-CDB conversion is mandatory where applicable; vector search, SQL Firewall enforcement, and Priority Transactions are separate decisions.
Select the exact target RU and verify platform support, client compatibility, feature restrictions, and licensing.
Rehearse upgrade and conversion with AutoUpgrade where appropriate.
Establish representative normal, peak, batch, and maintenance performance baselines.
Validate recovery and fallback independently. A successful upgrade does not prove recoverability.
Rehearse security and HA behavior, including rare operations, audit collection, service relocation, client retry, and post-failover backups.

The decision is not simply whether 23ai has more features. It is whether its architectural requirements and operational capabilities improve your environment enough to justify the migration, testing, and runbook changes.

This can reduce grant-maintenance work as objects change. However, schema-wide access can still exceed an account’s requirements. Review access by business role rather than mechanically reproducing historical grants.



Unified auditing is not new in 23ai. The important change is the desupport of traditional auditing, with specific treatment of existing settings during upgrades. Existing settings may continue to be honored in an upgraded environment; this is not a reason to retain the old model indefinitely.
Review:

Traditional audit settings and equivalent unified policies.
Audit-trail collection and retention.
SIEM or Audit Vault integration.
Audit volume after changes.
Procedures for policy administration.

23ai also adds unified auditing of individual columns in tables and views, enabling more targeted policies.



Validate both permitted and rejected behavior. A successful login does not prove that privileges, audit records, and firewall policy are correct.
Include scheduled jobs, reporting accounts, support access, deployment tools, and emergency administration in testing.
References:

Oracle SQL Firewall FAQ
Unified audit best-practice guidelines

title: 19c vs. 23ai for DBAs
text:
RMAN remains the foundation for physical backup and recovery. The changes evolve existing workflows rather than replace RMAN with an AI backup engine.



Oracle documents AES-256 in XTS mode for new encrypted backups when COMPATIBLE is set to 23.0.0 or higher, while retaining compatibility with previously configured algorithms.
Distinguish two decisions:

A stronger encryption default does not automatically encrypt all backups.
Changing compatibility and changing encryption configuration are separate operations.

Validate wallet or key access, recovery-host readiness, and restore compatibility rather than relying only on the backup job’s exit status.



23ai introduces a separate destination for Flashback Database logs using:
DB_FLASHBACK_LOG_DEST
DB_FLASHBACK_LOG_DEST_SIZE
Oracle documents disabling and reenabling Flashback logging when changing the destination. Plan the operation around recovery requirements and verify the exact target RU’s procedure.
The benefit is independent placement and capacity management. The consequence is another recovery-critical destination to monitor: an FRA-only dashboard is no longer the complete storage picture.



Oracle’s 23ai RMAN guidance describes:

Oracle-supplied backup modules and aliases.
Configuration support for OCI immutable buckets.
Copying backup sets between SBT destinations.
Simplified transport and platform-migration workflows.
Improved diagnostics and catalog-operation resilience.

Not every convenience is exclusive to 23ai. For example, Oracle notes that the Recovery Appliance backup module is also included starting with 19c RU 19.27. Compare exact RUs, not just major-version names.



Retest with the actual target software and infrastructure:

Restore to an alternate host.
Recover to a required point in time.
Restore encrypted backups using the intended key-management process.
Validate individual-PDB recovery where needed.
Confirm cloud or media-manager integration.

Transport-based migration has workflow-specific limitations. Oracle’s documented PDB transport workflow includes same-endian and local-undo requirements. Do not generalize one supported path into unrestricted cross-platform PDB transport.

RMAN 23ai new features, part 1
RMAN 23ai new features, part 2

title: 19c vs. 23ai for DBAs
text:
Conventional Data Guard protects the CDB as a database. Data Guard per PDB offers more granular protection and role transitions for individual pluggable databases.
This matters when consolidated applications have different availability requirements. A selected PDB can be the unit of protection and role transition rather than treating all PDBs as one application service.
Data Guard per PDB originated in the 21c line and was enhanced in 23ai. It is a difference from 19c, not a feature first invented in 23ai.



Review:

Source and destination CDB infrastructure.
PDB-specific protection and apply state.
Application services and reconnection.
Backup policies after role transitions.
Recovery objectives for each application.

Do not assume feature parity with every conventional Data Guard or Active Data Guard configuration. Validate the exact RU’s restrictions, topology, and licensing requirements.



Automatic Transaction Quarantine isolates problematic transaction recovery so the database can remain available while other work continues. Alerts and diagnostics still require investigation.







Feature
Problem addressed




Priority Transactions
A lower-priority transaction holds row locks that block higher-priority work.


Automatic Transaction Quarantine
A transaction encounters a problematic failure during transaction recovery.



One is a workload policy; the other is a fault-containment mechanism. Neither removes the need to diagnose the underlying cause.



Expand testing beyond startup:

Switchover and failover at the intended protection scope.
Client reconnection and transaction retries.
Backups after role transitions.
Recovery monitoring and alert routing.
Service ownership and operational handoffs.

Measure availability end to end, not merely by whether an instance or PDB is open.

Data Guard new features

What to revise for 23ai




Morning health checks
Identify CDB/PDB scope and inspect applicable recovery, quarantine, and workload-policy alerts.


Access provisioning
Consider schema privileges while preserving least privilege.


Application releases
Review SQL Firewall policies when enabled.


Performance troubleshooting
Separate ordinary SQL regressions from vector pressure and priority-driven rollback.


Capacity planning
Include vector resources and separate Flashback destinations where configured.


Backup monitoring
Review recoverability, encryption keys, and destination accessibility, not just completion.


DR exercises
Test the actual CDB-level or PDB-level protection model and client behavior.

Make jobs container-aware and validate features against the installed RU.



Not every item applies to every deployment. Existing monitoring and troubleshooting skills remain essential; new features add context rather than eliminate the need for fundamentals.

title: 19c vs. 23ai for DBAs
text:
Inventory 19c: architecture, RU, options, services, auditing, backups, and HA topology.
Separate required changes from optional adoption. Non-CDB conversion is mandatory where applicable; vector search, SQL Firewall enforcement, and Priority Transactions are separate decisions.
Select the exact target RU and verify platform support, client compatibility, feature restrictions, and licensing.
Rehearse upgrade and conversion with AutoUpgrade where appropriate.
Establish representative normal, peak, batch, and maintenance performance baselines.
Validate recovery and fallback independently. A successful upgrade does not prove recoverability.
Rehearse security and HA behavior, including rare operations, audit collection, service relocation, client retry, and post-failover backups.

The decision is not simply whether 23ai has more features. It is whether its architectural requirements and operational capabilities improve your environment enough to justify the migration, testing, and runbook changes.
